paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brown took place shortly after midnight on October 19, 1888, when a mob of several hundred men went to the county jail at Moorhead, Minnesota, to hang Brown, a prisoner accused of shooting a Moorhead policeman. Sheriff Jensen had removed Brown earlier in the evening, and the mob dispersed after a committee searched the jail and failed to find him. The episode was reported in papers from Minnesota to Montana and Michigan, mostly in a wire version that placed the mob at Fargo, and a second threatened lynching at Moorhead followed in November.

According to the St. Paul Daily Globe's Moorhead correspondent, Fargo police suspected a man known as Murphy of a robbery at the Manitoba house in Fargo and sent Officer Benson over to Moorhead to arrest him at a dance at Erickson's hall. Murphy drew a revolver, marched Benson and Moorhead officer John Thompson down to the street, and shot Officer Pete Poull through the heart when Poull ran up, at about 12:30 a.m. on October 18. Thompson exchanged shots with him and brought him down with several wounds, and he was carried to the county jail in critical condition.

Later reports named the prisoner as Thomas Brown, alias Murphy. A Fargo-side paragraph called him "a professional crook" suspected of several burglaries and said there had been "strong talk of lynching" through the day.

Anticipating trouble, Sheriff Jensen and a deputy took Brown from the jail in a carriage on Thursday evening and drove several miles into the country, where they stayed the night. Shortly after midnight a mob that the Globe counted at 400 and the wire at 500 reached the jail, carrying railroad iron, jackscrews and sledge hammers to batter the walls. The wire account described the men as "maddened by liquor" and said they would have hanged the prisoner had he been there.

A deputy at the jail door proposed that the crowd choose a committee to search the building, and once the committee was satisfied that Brown was gone the mob dispersed. Early the next morning the sheriff boarded a train with Brown at Tenney, a flag station six miles east of Moorhead, and lodged him in the Hennepin county jail at Minneapolis.

No arrests of mob members were reported, although on November 2 Fargo police arrested Ben Bennett, alias James Kelley, as Brown's suspected partner. Brown was later brought back to Moorhead, and on the night of November 20 rumors that friends of Poull would lead a mob at 3 a.m. led the sheriff to remove him again. By mid-December he was held quietly in the Otter Tail county jail at Fergus Falls, recovered from his wounds, and was quoted as saying that without a change of venue from Clay County "I shall have to swing." His trial was set for the January term before Judge Mills, but no report of the trial or its outcome appears in the coverage.

Most papers outside Minnesota printed a short wire paragraph that placed the mob "at Fargo" and named the dead officer variously as Pobie, Poole or Poull. The Daily Yellowstone Journal headed it "Wanted a Necktie Social," and the Bismarck Weekly Tribune ran it under a Moorhead dateline with a headline about "Moorhead Men." Some versions added that many in the crowd were only spectators and that "the sheriff's action is commended."

The St. Paul Daily Globe, with a correspondent in Moorhead, gave the fullest coverage, from the shooting through the sheriff's flight to Minneapolis and the November scare, under headlines such as "A Murderer's Danger" and "Saved by a Sheriff." Its reports, like the wire's, called Brown "the murderer" without qualification, and none of the coverage mentioned his race. Short notices of the November removal ran in Minnesota and Dakota digests such as the Morris Tribune and the Reporter and Farmer.

The wire placed the mob at Fargo, Dakota Territory, while the Globe's Moorhead dispatches, filed within hours and naming Sheriff Jensen and the county jail, placed it at Moorhead. Accounts also differ on the crowd's size, given as 400, 500 or "several hundred," and on whether it gathered Thursday or Friday night.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brown
bases: A mob went to the Clay County jail at Moorhead to lynch a prisoner accused of killing a policeman and dispersed after a committee failed to find him (A2, A3, A4); it is an attempted lynching.

No one was killed: the sheriff removed Brown before a mob of 400 to 500 men reached the jail, and a second threatened mob in November was also forestalled (A2, A3, A13). The episode is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

Moorhead specials to the St. Paul Daily Globe (A2, A4) and an independent wire report carried in Montana, Dakota and Michigan papers (A3, A5, A9, A10) agree that a large mob sought the prisoner at the jail and that the sheriff had removed him, though they differ on the town.

accounts.gist: A mob of 400 went to the Moorhead county jail shortly after midnight; Sheriff Jensen had taken Murphy away in a hack and a committee found the jail empty.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A mob of 500, armed with railroad iron, jackscrews and sledges and 'maddened by liquor', organized at Fargo to lynch Brown; a deputy let a committee search the jail and the mob dispersed.

accounts.label: Fargo-side paragraph
accounts.gist: Strong talk of lynching all day; a crowd of several hundred carried a railroad tie to the jail but the prisoner had been removed.

framing.detail: Distant papers ran the wire paragraph under light headlines such as 'Wanted a Necktie Social' and called Brown 'the murderer', while noting that 'the sheriff's action is commended'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe's Moorhead specials ran 'A Murderer's Danger' and 'Saved by a Sheriff', treating Brown's guilt as settled and the sheriff's removals as the story.
The New Ulm Review paragraph described Brown as 'a professional crook' and said a lynching 'would surprise no one'.

versions.value: The county jail at Moorhead, Minn.

conflicts.note: The Globe's Moorhead specials, written within hours and naming Sheriff Jensen and the Clay County jail, are better evidence; the Bismarck Tribune's wire copy carries a Moorhead dateline and 'Moorhead men' headline over text saying Fargo (A9).
No account reconciles the numbers; the wire adds that many were spectators (A5).
The Globe's 3 a.m. Oct. 19 dispatch fixes the mob in the early hours of Friday, October 19.
The local Globe gives Pete Poull.
